headline: Uganda and Conservation Group Partner to Save Rare Tree-Climbing Lions
meta_description: Uganda Wildlife Authority and Wildlife Conservation Society sign 10-year deal to co-manage Queen Elizabeth National Park's threatened lion population.
summary_short: A new partnership aims to save Uganda's endangered tree-climbing lions through community support and better wildlife protection.
body:
Uganda's Wildlife Authority and the Wildlife Conservation Society have signed a historic 10-year agreement to jointly manage the Ishasha Sector of Queen Elizabeth National Park, home to the iconic tree-climbing lions that once drew visitors from around the world. Under the partnership, WCS will oversee biodiversity management, community engagement, and tourist development across the 500-square-kilometer region, while Uganda retains law enforcement duties. The collaboration addresses an urgent crisis: lion numbers in the park have collapsed by more than 90% since the late 1970s, from 400 individuals down to just 39 today. Fewer than five lions now remain in Ishasha itself.

The decline stems from overlapping threats that have poisoned the relationship between wildlife protection and local communities. Herders have retaliated against lions that attack livestock, and poachers have set snares throughout the park. A poisoned lion carcass killed at least six animals in 2021 alone. WCS plans to rebuild trust by hiring "lion guardians" and scouts from surrounding towns, while also funding livestock enclosures and water boreholes to reduce conflict. The organization has committed to extensive community consultations in its first six months.

Beyond conservation, the partnership addresses serious governance concerns. A 2024 investigation documented credible allegations of extrajudicial killings and violence by park rangers. WCS's agreement includes new human rights protections, grievance structures, and a code of conduct—measures both organizations say will strengthen accountability while protecting both people and wildlife. This collaborative approach signals a broader shift across Africa: governments and conservation groups working together to manage parks in ways that respect both nature and the communities living alongside it.
quick_facts: Uganda Wildlife Authority and Wildlife Conservation Society sign 10-year co-management deal
Lion population in Queen Elizabeth Park dropped 90% since late 1970s: 400 to 39 individuals
Ishasha Sector covers 500 square kilometers of the 1,978 km² park
WCS will hire local "lion guardians" and build livestock enclosures to reduce human-wildlife conflict
Agreement includes human rights protections and grievance structures for rangers
